questions.stem: What does 'WWW' stand for?
questions.explanation: WWW stands for World Wide Web — a system of interlinked hypertext documents and resources accessed via the internet using browsers. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. Note: the Web is a service running on the Internet; the two terms are not identical.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which of the following is a web browser?
questions.explanation: Google Chrome is a web browser — software used to access and display web pages. Google (the search engine) is a website/service accessed THROUGH a browser; Gmail is an email service; Windows is an operating system. Other browsers include Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'URL' stand for?
questions.explanation: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator — the address of a resource on the web, e.g., https://www.example.com/page. It specifies the protocol (https), domain name, and path. The URL is what you type into a browser's address bar to visit a specific page.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a search engine?
questions.explanation: Google is a search engine — a service that lets users find information on the web by entering keywords. Other search engines include Bing, Yahoo, and DuckDuckGo. Outlook is an email client, Photoshop is image-editing software, and Excel is a spreadsheet application.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: In an email, what does 'CC' stand for?
questions.explanation: CC stands for Carbon Copy — recipients in the CC field receive a copy of the email, and all recipients can see who was CC'd. BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) hides the BCC recipients from others. The terms derive from the carbon paper once used to make copies of typed letters.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Who is credited with inventing the World Wide Web?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist at CERN, invented the World Wide Web in 1989, along with HTML, HTTP, and the first browser. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn are known as 'fathers of the Internet' for designing the TCP/IP protocol — a distinct contribution from the Web itself.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'HTTP' stand for?
questions.explanation: HTTP stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol — the protocol used to transfer web pages between a web server and a browser. HTTPS (HTTP Secure) adds encryption (SSL/TLS) for secure communication. The protocol appears at the start of web URLs.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: The 'S' in HTTPS indicates that the connection is:
questions.explanation: The 'S' in HTTPS stands for Secure. HTTPS encrypts data exchanged between the browser and server using SSL/TLS, protecting against eavesdropping and tampering. A padlock icon in the browser's address bar typically indicates a secure HTTPS connection — important for banking and login pages.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'IP' stand for in the context of IP address?
questions.explanation: IP stands for Internet Protocol. An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to each device on a network, used to identify and locate it, e.g., 192.168.1.1 (IPv4). IPv6 is the newer version with a much larger address space. ISP (Internet Service Provider) is a different term.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which language is primarily used to create the structure of web pages?
questions.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language used to create the structure and content of web pages. CSS styles them, and JavaScript adds interactivity. SQL is for databases; Python and C++ are general-purpose programming languages (Python is also used for web backends).
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What is a 'cookie' in the context of web browsing?

options.text: A small file stored by a website on the user's computer to remember information

questions.explanation: A cookie is a small text file that a website stores on the user's computer/browser to remember information such as login status, preferences, or items in a shopping cart. Cookies enable personalised experiences but raise privacy considerations. They are not viruses, though they can be used for tracking.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: In a URL, what does the domain extension '.gov' typically indicate?
questions.explanation: The '.gov' domain extension indicates a government organisation. Other common top-level domains (TLDs): .com (commercial), .edu (educational), .org (organisation/non-profit), .net (network), and country codes like .in (India). India's government sites often use .gov.in.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'ISP' stand for?
questions.explanation: ISP stands for Internet Service Provider — a company that provides internet access to customers, such as Jio, Airtel, or BSNL in India. The ISP connects your home or office network to the wider internet, typically assigning you a public IP address.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which protocol is used to send email?
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used to SEND email. To RECEIVE email, POP3 (Post Office Protocol) or IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) are used. FTP transfers files; HTTP transfers web pages; TCP is a transport-layer protocol underlying many of these.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'download' mean?

options.text: Sending data from your computer to a remote server
Receiving/transferring data from a remote server to your computer

questions.explanation: Download means receiving or transferring data FROM a remote server TO your local computer (e.g., saving a file from a website). The opposite is upload — sending data from your computer to a server (e.g., posting a photo). Direction relative to the user's device is the key distinction.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What is the function of a 'hyperlink' on a web page?

options.text: To connect to and navigate to another document or web page when clicked

questions.explanation: A hyperlink (link) is a clickable element that navigates the user to another web page, document, or location when clicked. Hyperlinks are the foundation of the Web's interconnected structure (hence 'HyperText'). They are usually shown as underlined or coloured text, or as buttons/images.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which of the following is an email service provider?
questions.explanation: Gmail (by Google) is an email service provider. Firefox is a web browser, Bing is a search engine, and Linux is an operating system. Other email services include Outlook/Hotmail, Yahoo Mail, and ProtonMail.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'Wi-Fi' enable?

options.text: Wireless local area networking to connect devices to the internet

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi enables wireless local area networking, allowing devices like laptops and smartphones to connect to a network/internet without cables, using radio waves (based on IEEE 802.11 standards). A wireless router broadcasts the Wi-Fi signal within its range.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: A 'web server' is best described as:

options.text: A device used to print web pages
A program/computer that stores web pages and delivers them to browsers on request

questions.explanation: A web server is a computer (and software) that stores website files and delivers web pages to clients (browsers) when requested over HTTP/HTTPS. Examples of web server software include Apache and Nginx. The browser is the 'client' that requests and displays the pages — the client-server model.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'spam' refer to in the context of email?

options.text: Unsolicited bulk/junk email sent to many recipients

questions.explanation: Spam refers to unsolicited bulk (junk) email, often advertising or fraudulent, sent indiscriminately to many recipients. Email services use spam filters to detect and divert such messages to a 'Spam' or 'Junk' folder. Phishing emails (which attempt to steal information) are a dangerous subset of unwanted mail.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Internet from the World Wide Web?

options.text: The Internet is the global network of connected computers; the Web is a service of interlinked documents that runs on top of the Internet
They are exactly the same thing
The Web is the network of cables; the Internet is the collection of websites
The Internet only carries email, while the Web carries everything else

questions.explanation: The Internet is the vast global infrastructure of interconnected computer networks (hardware, cables, protocols like TCP/IP). The World Wide Web is one service that runs ON the Internet — a system of interlinked hypertext documents accessed via browsers using HTTP. Other Internet services include email (SMTP), file transfer (FTP), and streaming. So the Web is a subset of what the Internet enables.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What is 'phishing'?

options.text: A legitimate method of online banking
A fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information by disguising as a trustworthy entity in electronic communication
A technique to speed up internet connections

questions.explanation: Phishing is a cyber-fraud technique where attackers impersonate trustworthy entities (banks, companies) via fake emails, messages, or websites to trick victims into revealing sensitive data like passwords, OTPs, or card numbers. Warning signs include urgent language, suspicious links, and requests for confidential information. Never share OTPs or click unverified links.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: Which protocol translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses?
questions.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-friendly domain names (like google.com) into numerical IP addresses that computers use to locate each other. It acts like the internet's phonebook. DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices; FTP transfers files; SMTP sends email. DNS resolution happens behind the scenes whenever you visit a website.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What is the main difference between IPv4 and IPv6?

options.text: IPv4 is wireless while IPv6 is wired
IPv6 can only be used for email
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses providing a vastly larger address space than IPv4's 32-bit addresses

questions.explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (e.g., 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334), providing about 3.4×10^38 addresses — an enormous space — compared to IPv4's 32-bit addresses (~4.3 billion), which have been exhausted. IPv6 was developed to solve IPv4 address depletion as internet-connected devices multiplied. Both are versions of the Internet Protocol.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge

questions.stem: What does 'cloud computing' primarily refer to?

options.text: Computing performed only during cloudy weather
A method of cooling computer servers using water vapour
Delivering computing services (storage, servers, software) over the internet, on demand, instead of local hardware
Computing that works only without an internet connection

questions.explanation: Cloud computing delivers computing services — storage, servers, databases, software — over the internet ('the cloud') on an on-demand, pay-as-you-go basis, rather than relying on local hardware. Examples include Google Drive (storage), AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. Service models include IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
